data.reason: The KPI names volume first: deliver as many orders as possible within the promised times. It then adds a fairness condition: leave no company's customers behind. Option 1 keeps that order. The main goal is on_time_deliveries. min_company_on_time_rate is watched, which protects the weakest company directly. Option 3 instead watches on_time_rate_gap, and the gap can improve when the best company gets worse, which does not help any customer. Option 2 would make the weakest company's rate the binding goal. It could reject amendments that add many on-time deliveries for customers, and the KPI does not rank fairness above volume. Watching unfinished catches the risk that orders already going to be late get abandoned. The KPI gives no numeric levels, so I set no targets or guards. Fairness is therefore monitored, not enforced. If an amendment raises the town-wide count while lowering the weakest company's rate, the trade-off should come back to a human decision. Contract (DELIVERY_SLA) relaxations must not be used to inflate on-time counts. Any regulation revision must state its effect on A, B, C and on customers. No measurements exist yet, so no table values are cited.
assumptions: Under the same seed the order count is fixed, so on_time_deliveries ranks amendments the same way on_time_rate does.
min_company_on_time_rate is computed per company over that company's own orders, so it reflects each company's customers.
The operator did not intend fairness to override volume, given the KPI's word order.
unknowns: How large the current differences between companies' on-time rates are.
How much of a drop in the weakest company's rate the operator would accept for a town-wide gain.
Whether unfinished orders are currently a meaningful share of demand.
